item.title: Why treating soil acidity crop by crop is no longer enough for prairie farmers
item.description: To protect their future harvests, Western Canadian farmers need to manage soil acidity across their entire multiyear rotation rather than crop by crop, long-term research from the University of Alberta suggests. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
item.description: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation […] Fuente: The Verge.

item.title: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer
item.description: For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Polar vortex faltering weeks earlier than ever recorded
item.description: Meteorologists said Friday they were observing an unprecedented early disruption of the polar vortex, raising the risk of cold snaps across the Northern Hemisphere, though there remains significant uncertainty. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pakistani astronaut to board Shenzhou 24 and become the first foreigner on China's space station
item.description: A Pakistani astronaut will join the crew of China's Shenzhou 24 spacecraft on a mission that would make him the first foreign national to board Beijing's space station, state media reported Saturday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discovered an unknown baby right whale off Canada. They say it's a cause for joy
item.description: PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Scientists who study whales are heartened by an unexpected discovery of a baby right whale off Canada. Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. Scientists with the New England […] Publicado también por: Mongabay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atlanta's new giant pandas will make their public debut after a 2-year absence
item.description: Zoo-goers watched two giant pandas loaned by China make their public debut Friday in Atlanta, where they will be hosted for the next 10 years. The pair joins the many pandas shipped to zoos around the world as part of Beijing's "panda diplomacy" program aimed at cultivating foreign ties. Publicado también por: Deutsche Welle - World, France 24 - English. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La NASA presenta X-70 Fractal, un nuevo avión experimental que probará maniobras "nunca antes demostradas" con piloto a bordo
item.description: La NASA acaba de desvelar un nuevo avión experimental con piloto a bordo y la verdad es que deja con la boca abierta por lo que puede hacer: no es un avión de pasajeros ni tampoco un caza, sino una plataforma de investigación en vuelo que permitirá estudiar cómo responde una aeronave en situaciones de maniobra que, según la Administración Nacional de Aeronáutica y del Espacio, nunca antes se han demostrado en un vuelo tripulado. Un laboratorio con alas . El X-70 Fractal será el último de una saga, los aviones X, que la NASA emplea para probar tecnologías antes de que lleguen a la aviación… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Eva R. de Luis

item.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
item.description: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
item.description: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
item.description: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
item.description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls
item.description: Researchers say popular performers covertly market OnlyFans content and tell followers about wealthy lifestyle TikTok is helping to promote and normalise the sex industry, allowing “sexfluencers” to post videos aimed at marketing pornographic content they have uploaded elsewhere on sites such as OnlyFans, a report indicates. After studying non-explicit content posted on TikTok over the course of a year by some of OnlyFans’ most popular young female performers, researchers said the women buried coded references to pornography in “girly lifestyle content” that showed them shopping, playing with… Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: China acaba de conseguir algo extraordinario en su estación espacial: ha enfriado átomos hasta un récord histórico
item.description: El frío tiene un límite que la física conoce muy bien, pero al que ningún laboratorio puede llegar exactamente: el cero absoluto . Cuanto más nos acercamos a él, más difícil resulta reducir la energía térmica de los átomos, hasta el punto de que cada pequeño descenso de temperatura representa un desafío experimental. Y lo interesante no es solo alcanzar una cifra extraordinariamente baja, sino lo que sucede con la materia en esas condiciones. A temperaturas tan extremas, comienzan a manifestarse fenómenos cuánticos que normalmente permanecen ocultos por la agitación térmica. Desde la órbita… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Untangling the patterns of the cosmic microwave background to better understand the early universe
item.description: A figure in red trudges across a blanket of white. Snow squeaks under the scientist's feet, too dry to be slick or soft. Only a line of flags and a few large buildings—the scientist's destination—break up the landscape. The sun hovers on the horizon, never quite setting against a blue sky devoid of clouds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease
item.description: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia, a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system, by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, although clinical trials are still needed to establish its effectiveness in patients. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Spot a baby bird on the ground? Don't be tempted to bird‑nap it
item.description: Spring is the season of blooming flowers and buzzing bees. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The wasps that horrified Darwin reveal evolution's one-way streets
item.description: Few insects have a more gruesome lifestyle than Darwin wasps. Rather than simply hunting other animals, these parasitic wasps lay their eggs on or inside living hosts, including caterpillars, beetles and spiders. Their larvae then feed on their hosts, gradually consuming them and eventually killing them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
item.description: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat ultraviolet focusing mirrors for compact optics
item.description: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces. Metasurfaces can achieve similar functions with a flat layer of nanoscale structures that locally control the phase of light. Extending these flat optics into the ultraviolet could support compact systems for high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it introduces a fundamental materials problem: many of the materials used to make metasurfaces strongly absorb UV light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Tras completar con éxito el histórico sobrevuelo lunar, se conoció una frase que la astronauta de la NASA pronunció mientras realizaba la misión Artemis II Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.description: The rocket and satellite-internet company is looking to challenge telecom giants. Fuente: MarketWatch.

item.title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
item.description: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism. The essential amino acid tryptophan binds to a second site on the enzyme TDO2, distinct from where it is consumed. This sequesters a region needed by two effectors, the kinase CK2 and the ubiquitin ligase CUL1–β-TrCP, which act sequentially to signal TDO2… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
item.description: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New research rules out the theory of Stonehenge Altar Stone's Northeast Scottish Origin
item.description: Researchers continue to explore the origins of the Altar Stone at Stonehenge, which weighs approximately six tonnes. Recent studies suggested a possible origin from northeast Scotland, but findings have complicated this theory. A new international team's research found no matching source from the Scottish locations they examined, narrowing possibilities down. Previous assumptions about the Altar Stone's Welsh origins have been challenged by new geological insights. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: New method measures microplastics in the air using an uncrewed aerial system
item.description: Microplastics have been found in our bodies and the food we eat—and even in remote environments around the world, including seawater and ice in the Arctic. Despite their prevalence, little is known about how they move through the atmosphere. New CIRES-led research, which demonstrates a new method for sampling microplastics in the atmosphere using an uncrewed aerial system (UAS), aims to change that. The findings are published in the journal Scientific Reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Future warming events will outdo the extreme heat waves of the recent past, new study finds
item.description: The extreme heat waves we have seen over the last few years may only serve as a preview of what is to come as a result of climate change. A new study led by researcher Philipp Aglas-Leitner from Freie Universität Berlin, published in Nature Communications, finds that future heat waves could last longer, impact larger areas, and be much more severe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-powered method resurrects 'dead-end' compounds for drug discovery
item.description: Throughout the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never go on to become medicines. A Florida State University researcher is part of a team that has discovered a new way to give some of these "dead ends" a second chance at becoming the foundation for tomorrow's blockbuster drugs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum gas microscope reveals individual atoms in first tunable three-component Hubbard system
item.description: For the first time, an international team of researchers from Germany, Thailand, India, China and the United States has created a three-component Hubbard system with tunable interactions in the laboratory. In doing so, the team used a quantum gas microscope to make the individual atoms visible. The study, published in Science, provides an important foundation for future quantum simulations of nuclear physics and materials science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European forests need to solve two crises—but not necessarily in one place
item.description: Forest areas can act both as carbon sinks and as vital habitats for thousands of species—but not necessarily at the same time. This has important implications for how Europe should manage its forests, says a University of Copenhagen researcher. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MTG-I2 satellite delivers remarkable first images, capturing a weather view of Europe every 2.5 minutes
item.description: Europe's meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT, has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite's launch on Aug. 27, 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes. This unprecedented frequency will help forecasters monitor fast-developing weather hazards more closely and support earlier, more precise warnings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: High-precision timeline helps clarify an ancient magma surge in the North Cascades
item.description: Where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, belts of volcanoes known as continental arcs can form. Located around the world, these arcs may undergo episodic magma flare-ups—dramatic surges in the flow of magma into the continental crust at rates up to 20 times higher than normal. However, what triggers these extreme surges, which last tens of millions of years, can be unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI won't ever make a historically accurate film—but it could help archaeology create better stories
item.description: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer's "Odyssey" by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticized for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story "historically accurate and true to the art of Homer" at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI points researchers toward new disease targets hidden in mitochondria
item.description: Artificial intelligence is helping Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists fast-track answers to a long-standing question in human biology: What do hundreds of mystery proteins in the mitochondria actually do? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’
item.description: The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised. Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Ian Sample Science editor

item.title: Redefining honesty in a crisis: Why truth alone is not enough
item.description: When a company suffers a cyberattack, leaks customer data or faces a major public scandal, telling the truth is essential. But new research suggests it is not enough on its own: organizations also need to communicate early, treat people with respect and show how they intend to put things right. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Mega heat waves' strengthened by interaction between soil moisture, atmospheric pressure and temperature
item.description: A new study has found that a self-reinforcing interaction between temperature, soil moisture and atmospheric pressure is being triggered at high temperatures, making extreme heat waves 10% hotter than they would otherwise be. The study was published in Science Advances and led by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fruit fly study offers clues to insect survival in a hotter, drier world
item.description: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute have identified a specialized lipid barrier in the fruit fly pupa that protects against dehydration in dry and hot environments. Their findings also expose the lipid barrier's limit, suggesting that insects in some regions of the world may struggle to adapt to climate change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Security researchers found hundreds of servers hosting the penetration testing tool Artex exposed to the internet, allowing anyone access to the hacking tool. Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Zack Whittaker

item.title: Beyond trial and error: A framework for AI-driven solid-electrolyte discovery
item.description: A battery material can look perfect in the lab and still fail in a real battery. That is the puzzle facing researchers working on solid electrolytes, the materials seen as key to safer, longer-lasting batteries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smart packaging film 'lights up' under UV as meat loses freshness
item.description: Food spoilage causes chemical changes that are not always easy to detect by appearance alone. To provide a clearer indication of freshness and quality, researchers at Kyushu University have developed a smart packaging film that changes color and glows under ultraviolet (UV) light as meat loses freshness. Tested with refrigerated mutton, the film responds to compounds released during spoilage, offering two ways to track changes in food quality. The findings are published in the Chemical Engineering Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: You know the launch market is tough when satellite companies start building rockets
item.description: "The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Noise pollution changes biology or behavior in 80% of animal species studied
item.description: We live in a noisy world. Whether it is the roar of traffic, the rumble of ships or the hum of heavy industry, there is often no escaping noise unless you are a hermit on a desert island. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SynFit guides enzyme engineering by balancing several useful traits at once
item.description: Enzymes are biology's tiny chemists. They help build, break and rearrange molecules quickly and precisely. In the lab, scientists have long put enzymes to work making useful chemicals. But nature's enzymes cannot do every reaction a researcher might want. Sometimes scientists need an enzyme to take on a job it did not evolve to do. That's where enzyme engineering comes in—researchers make changes to an enzyme, test how those changes affect what the enzyme does and look for versions that work better. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'I heard a barnacle'—how paying attention to nature's background noise can reveal animal secrets
item.description: During four days on Washington's Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot, a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook. Any one of them could have been the trip's highlight. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Vibrating mirrors of light create analog of a black hole event horizon
item.description: Optical cavities are pairs of light-trapping mirrors and underpin the operation of lasers, atomic clocks and many types of precision sensors. If the distance between the mirrors is changed rapidly enough, some theories predict that the waves inside them should bunch together into short, intense pulses. So far, however, this prediction has never been tested directly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The John Lewis Christmas ad captures the deep need for grandmothers
item.description: Like many of us, I always enjoy the John Lewis Christmas ad and 2026 is no different. This year, I love the fact that the star of the show is a grandmother. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atom-scale model could help improve material growth for advanced electronics
item.description: Penn State researchers have refined an atom-scale model of how silicon carbide changes from a solid into vapor during crystal growth, work that could help manufacturers produce higher-quality material for advanced electronics while reducing costly trial-and-error experiments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: States tax sports betting heavily, but gamblers may barely feel it
item.description: Sports betting has grown explosively since 2018, when a U.S. Supreme Court ruling struck down a federal ban on it. Now, Americans wager more than $165 billion on sports annually, contributing to an industry larger than state-run lotteries even excluding prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket. Fuente: Phys.org.

Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. item.description: Blue Origin tiene que intentar destacar después de que su plataforma de lanzamiento se incendiara con la explosión de un cohete New Glenn . La compañía de Jeff Bezos quiere demostrar que sigue siendo de las más punteras de la industria espacial. Por eso, acaba de presentar un motor para sus cohetes que promete ser mucho más potente, pero a un 25% del precio de fabricación habitual. Northstar . Así se llama el motor que complementará y con el tiempo sustituirá al tradicional BE-4 de la primera etapa de los cohetes de Blue Origin. Tiene la mitad de piezas , un 30% menos de masa y alrededor del… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Scientists achieve record-breaking low temperature on China's space station, paving the way for new physics experiments
item.description: Matter starts to behave differently at extremely low temperatures, creating conditions ideal for studying quantum physics and new states of matter. Now, researchers from China have achieved a new low-temperature record aboard their Tiangong space station. Their research, recently published in Science, might lead to a new generation of experiments in quantum physics and precision measurements in space. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Evolutionary history and genetic basis of spruce diversification revealed
item.description: The genus Picea (spruce) is widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere and is a dominant component of boreal and montane forests. Understanding the evolutionary processes that have shaped diversification and regional differentiation across the genus requires a well-resolved phylogeny of Picea. However, the evolutionary history of Picea has long been obscure due to conflicting genetic signals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers establish G0 founder population carrying targeted mutations in marine mollusks
item.description: Although genome-editing-based breeding has advanced rapidly in aquaculture, progress in marine mollusks has lagged behind. The main challenge is not genome editing itself, but rather rearing the few edited larvae through metamorphosis to establish a viable G0 founder population. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Technique that spots tRNAs in action could accelerate drug development for inherited diseases
item.description: Human cells turn genetic instructions into proteins with great precision. Critical for the translation of this information are transfer RNAs, or tRNAs, small molecules that read the genetic code three letters at a time and bring the matching building blocks of proteins, the amino acids, to the cell's protein-making machinery, the ribosome. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: M30’s Sparkling Stars
item.description: This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image released Nov. 5, 2026, provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier, who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: New method for upcycling polyethylene is suitable for mass production as a raw material for nylon
item.description: It would greatly benefit the environment and climate if nylon—chemically known as polyamide—could be produced on a large scale from plastic waste in the future, rather than from petroleum, as has been the norm until now. At LIKAT in Rostock, chemists pursuing this approach have succeeded in selectively converting polyethylene—the main component of all plastic waste—into dicarboxylic acids, which can serve as chemical precursors for nylon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robot successfully builds space structure in first autonomous construction demo
item.description: A robotic truss builder that was conceived, designed and built by Caltech researchers has successfully built a structure in space—without the help of astronauts—for the first time. The truss builder, part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, consists of an autonomous manipulator that picks up struts and joints held in nearby dispensers to repeatedly assemble identical sections, or bays, of a perimeter truss. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New 3D microscope packs many imaging tools into one system
item.description: An international team of researchers led by UT Southwestern Medical Center has developed a versatile light-sheet microscope that captures 3D views of biological samples, from activity inside living cells to larger tissues. Designed to make detailed imaging much simpler and faster, the approach could help laboratories stretch equipment budgets and expand research that may ultimately inform patient care. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: World-first successful wild release of endangered broad-headed snake
item.description: The broad-headed snake (Hoplocephalus bungaroides), one of Australia's most endangered snakes, has been given a lifeline, with at least four of six captive-bred juveniles surviving the critical first few months after their release into the wild. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny biodegradable particles poke openings in skin to boost topical drug delivery
item.description: Skin is remarkably good at keeping things out of the body. Typically, that's a positive. It becomes an issue when medicine needs to get in. Swallow a pill to treat a skin condition, and the medicine enters your stomach, moves into your bloodstream and travels throughout your body—all to reach a problem in your skin. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Oh boy, all girls again: Research tracks sea turtle sex ratios
item.description: Forty young sea turtles recently reached an important milestone at Florida Atlantic University: They were finally big enough to leave the university's marine science laboratory and return to the ocean. Their release was a reason to celebrate. But for FAU researchers who have spent years studying loggerhead, leatherback and green sea turtle hatchlings, there is a growing concern about what the next generation of sea turtles may look like: They're almost all girls. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The spring mountain butterfly has been spotted for the first time beneath power lines
item.description: The Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB) for the first time has detected the presence of the spring mountain butterfly (Erebia epistygne), a species under threat of extinction in Catalonia, under the electricity transmission lines of Red Eléctrica, Spain's transmission system operator. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mineral-forming method removes more than 99% of radioactive technetium from liquid waste
item.description: Technetium-99 is a long-lived radioactive byproduct of nuclear fuel production and reprocessing. In many environments, it forms a highly mobile chemical species that can move readily through water and soil, making it a priority contaminant at legacy nuclear sites including Sellafield in the U.K. and Hanford in the United States. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beyond green claims: Understanding how consumers evaluate sustainable products
item.description: Sustainability has become an increasingly visible feature of consumer-packaged goods (CPGs), from the ingredients used in household products to the materials and design of their packaging. For companies marketing sustainable products, however, an important question remains: Does communicating more environmental benefits necessarily improve how consumers evaluate a product? Although highlighting several sustainability features may provide a more complete picture, consumers may not respond to all this information in the same way. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Release of largest dataset to date on wildlife in Europe
item.description: Every autumn for the last five years, hundreds of volunteers have set out remotely triggered cameras in mountains, forests, farms and beaches in more than 20 countries in Europe. Their joint project is called Snapshot Europe, and it's the largest open-access survey of mammals and birds across an entire continent. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From chaos to 'intelligent' soft matter—how tiny chemical differences guide droplets into ordered structures
item.description: Disorder can make sense, and understanding its logic can be genuinely useful. A study by a research group at the University of Trento shows how a minimal chemical difference can turn chaotic, disordered motion into a highly coordinated and reproducible structure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wacky magnetic fields of ice giants may stem from conductivity changes in their deep interiors
item.description: When NASA's Voyager 2 robotic probe flew by Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it uncovered an anomaly: their magnetic fields are highly disordered, unlike Earth's, which has well-defined north and south poles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why bandicoots and bilbies evolved such different snouts
item.description: Why does a quenda have a short, sturdy snout, while its relative the bilby has such a remarkably long one? New research led by Murdoch University's Harry Butler Institute suggests millions of years of adaptation to different environments across Australia and New Guinea may help explain the difference. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Paired but out of step: Why electron pairing alone is not enough for room-temperature superconductivity
item.description: Levitating trains, ultra-efficient energy storage, and quantum computers: superconductivity could unlock a wealth of possibilities for the future. New research led by scientists from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich has now shed light on one of the key requirements for achieving superconductivity at room temperature. Their findings, published in Science, bring scientists a step closer to understanding how this might be achieved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Higher grocery prices linked to worse food insufficiency, mental health
item.description: As grocery prices continue to rise, a study by researchers at Penn State found that in addition to increased spending, the price hikes are also associated with higher risk of food insufficiency and worse mental health conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket Report: Artemis II literally tore through the atmosphere; New Glenn delay
item.description: Interstellar Technologies announces more government funding for the Japanese Zero rocket. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: Social media could improve disaster aid coordination, review finds
item.description: A literature review in the International Journal of Services and Standards has highlighted the potential of social media to improve humanitarian supply chain management. However, it also identifies a shortage of research into its role in the delivery of aid during emergencies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 2026 'most likely' to be second-hottest year on record: EU monitor
item.description: The world is on track for 2026 to be the second-hottest year on record as an exceptionally strong El Niño weather pattern turbocharges human-driven global warming, the EU's climate monitor said Friday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A kill switch for epilepsy? China cuts seizures by 92.6% in first human chemogenetic trial
item.description: For people living with refractory epilepsy, the brain is like a city that can suffer a blackout any time lightning strikes. Without warning, an abnormal neural discharge can sweep through the intracranial circuits, leaving behind convulsions, loss of consciousness and years of lingering panic. Around one-third of epilepsy patients worldwide are completely unresponsive to existing medications, while traditional craniotomy resection surgery often carries the risk of irreversible neurological... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Shi Huang

item.title: How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
item.description: Note: Some spoilers for Control Resonant's "Recursions and Iterations" mission follow. One of Control Resonant's most memorable missions involves time travel - kind of. There are certainly multiple timelines intersecting, or maybe overlapping, or maybe running in parallel. As protagonist Dylan Faden, you meet some of the researchers who are trapped in and investigating these […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: Kallie Plagge

item.title: A galaxy nicknamed Misty Moons offers a glimpse of early star formation
item.description: Gravitational lensing is one of astronomy's best tricks for seeing the early universe. When a massive galaxy cluster sits in between the observer and a distant object, its gravity bends and magnifies the distant object's light, acting like a giant natural magnifying glass. Galaxies that would otherwise be too faint to spot suddenly come into view because of gravitational lensing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Emptying towns reveal links between state withdrawal and political radicalization in Eastern Europe
item.description: Across Europe, the 'emptying' of places abandoned by the state, capital and people is increasingly common. At the epicenter of this growing phenomenon are villages and towns in Eastern Europe and Russia, where the transition from socialism to capitalism has expelled people and places from investment and the care of the state—changes that, in some places, have been further intensified by war. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Autistic children benefited from online literacy instruction during COVID pandemic
item.description: Despite many obstacles presented by students being at home during COVID-19 lockdowns and restrictions, autistic children involved in a feasibility study still showed significant progress through online instruction. Flinders University's Professor Joanne Arciuli, who led the study, says that developing useful tools for this area of literacy teaching plugs a gap in autistic care. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Positive views of caregiving nearly double for dementia caregivers after support program
item.description: Chinese American family caregivers of people with dementia reported a greater sense of control and competence in their caregiving roles and more positive views of caregiving after taking part in a seven-week digital support program, researchers at George Mason University found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket launcher deal illustrates deepening Russia-Iran relations
item.description: Report of deal comes as top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei discusses developing cooperation treaty with Putin. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Beijing approves giant Long March 9 rocket for deep-space and lunar base runs
item.description: Beijing has given the go-ahead for the Long March 9, a super heavy rocket often seen as China’s answer to SpaceX’s Starship, weeks after the American megarocket first reached orbit, according to a lecture slide circulating online. The stainless-steel giant received official approval last month, according to the slide. At 110 metres (361 feet) tall and 10.6 metres wide, it will be the most powerful and expensive launcher China has ever built. The slide, presented in the northwestern city of Xian... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins
item.description: A study of nearly 5,800 adults found that heart scans measuring calcium buildup in the arteries led to the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, despite recommending statins to far fewer patients. Surprisingly, patients advised to take statins based on their scans were nearly three times as likely to stick with their medication, raising intriguing questions about how doctors should identify and treat heart disease risk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China puts DF missiles on display as flight bans fuel speculation about ICBM test
item.description: Chinese state media showcased several Dongfeng-series missiles on Thursday to mark a key anniversary, including the nuclear-capable DF-61 intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) and the rarely seen DF-100 long-range supersonic cruise missile. The coverage coincided with social media reports suggesting that the PLA Rocket Force might have conducted an inland ICBM test, potentially involving a ground-based mid-course missile interception, although neither activity has been officially... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Albee Zhang

item.title: Forests or underground storage? New metric compares risks of carbon removal projects
item.description: The risk of relying on uncertain carbon removal projects can now be quantified using a new standardized metric that can be applied across all such schemes, irrespective of the technology used. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can AI learn to understand nature? Scientists set out a roadmap for the future of ecology
item.description: An international team of scientists has outlined how a new generation of artificial intelligence models could transform our understanding of ecosystems and help predict their responses to environmental change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cancer-linked gene uses 'shortcut' to trigger cell division
item.description: Living cells are one of the few materials that can replicate themselves, and this is crucial for tissue development and recovery from injury or illness. But making sure cell division only happens at the right time is essential; otherwise, unregulated replication can lead to problems like cancer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
item.description: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
item.description: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese space firm builds wooden rocket nose cone for cheaper, frequent launches
item.description: Chinese commercial space firm Light Year Explorer has manufactured a rocket fairing with a wooden outer skin as part of the company’s push for lower-cost, mass-produced launch vehicles. The design of the protective shell uses low-density plywood formed into a smooth aerodynamic curve, supported by an internal metal framework to bear loads, according to the Jiangsu-based company. “This configuration matches traditional composite fairings in key performance areas such as weight, structural... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Holly Chik

item.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
item.description: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise
item.description: Full-fat dairy may not be the health villain it has long been portrayed as, according to a new study finding that three daily servings did not worsen weight, cholesterol, or insulin resistance over 12 weeks. Researchers also observed improvements in blood pressure and nutrient intake, raising questions about longstanding recommendations to choose low-fat dairy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 6 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Farewell […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
item.description: The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists examining dinosaur fossils report evidence of preserved red blood cells and collagen amino acids, a finding led by Curtin University that could change how researchers investigate ancient biological material
item.description: Palaeontologists found fossilised signs of dinosaur blood and collagen in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. These structures were discovered in a theropod dinosaur known as Aratasaurus museunacionali. Advanced techniques identified iron-containing heme and collagen, suggesting biological materials survived long periods. Researchers believe rapid burial in low-oxygen conditions contributed to preservation. This discovery opens new avenues for understanding dinosaur biology beyond skeletal remains. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: Adaptation isn't keeping up with global warming, UN warns
item.description: With global warming set to exceed 1.5°C, adaptation finance falls far short of needs, implementation is constrained by institutional barriers, and losses and damages are mounting, according to a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New species of sawfly described
item.description: Yale College junior Leah Mock did fieldwork in a remote quarry in western Colorado that exposes the 50-million-year-old Green River Formation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How mitochondria keep protein production moving
item.description: Researchers at Karolinska Institutet have discovered how a protein called TACO1 helps mitochondria produce proteins when the process encounters difficult sequences. The study, published in Nature Communications, provides new insights into a mechanism that is disrupted in some mitochondrial diseases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Research seeks to clarify assisted suicide practices in Germany and inform future regulation
item.description: Assisted suicide is morally and ethically controversial. Public debate on the topic tends to arise primarily when a high-profile case comes to light—as was most recently the case with the famous twins Alice and Ellen Kessler. While assisted suicide is permitted in Germany, it is scarcely regulated by law. Until now, there has been little scientifically validated data on the current practice of assisted suicide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can engineering solve the forever chemical problem?
item.description: Among the technical inquiries spanning topics like cyclodextrin polymers and mass spectrometry that were stacked in Damian Helbling's inbox was a question about four golden retrievers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden ecological risk from overlooked invasive crayfish species
item.description: A new study reveals narrow-clawed crayfish, an understudied invasive species in the U.K., to be as aggressive as the well-known signal crayfish. Fuente: Phys.org.
